title: Officials, advocates push ‘Easy Enrollment’ box on tax forms amid rising health care costs
summary: Federal tax credits that kept health insurance costs down for 190,000 Marylanders ended on Jan. 1, but state officials set aside funds to buffer the loss and are urging people to check a box on their tax forms to learn about the Easy Enrollment program.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 5, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 5, 2026

The end of 2025 meant the end of federal tax credits that helped keep health insurance costs down for some 190,000 Marylanders, but it wasn’t the end of all help for those policy holders.

The state, anticipating the possible loss of federal assistance, set aside millions this year and next. And state officials gathered Monday to urge people to take advantage of the state’s Easy Enrollment program, which could help families get connected to more affordable health care by checking a box on their state tax forms.

“As the clock struck midnight on Dec. 31, thousands of Marylanders greeted the New Year not with cheers, but with increased anxiety,” Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) said at the Center for Urban Families in Baltimore Monday. “With increased worry and concern at the prospect of going without health insurance because they are now facing higher health insurance premiums.”

Lierman joined other state officials and health care advocates to raise awareness of Easy Enrollment, which has helped thousands of Marylanders get connected to affordable insurance over the five years since its launch. Under the program, Marylanders can check a box on their state tax return saying they are interested in learning about their health care options through the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace.

GET THE MORNING HEADLINES.

The exchange then reaches out with information about available health insurance options and whether those households qualify for subsidies to bring those costs down further.

Advocates say Easy Enrollment is especially important due to the expiration of a popular COVID-19 era expansion of a federal tax credit under the Affordable Care Act, which will lead to a hike in health insurance costs. State fiscal analysts estimated that the expiration of the federal advanced premium tax credits would mean the loss of about $150 million to Maryland.

In anticipation of that, legislators created a state-based health insurance subsidies program, aimed at countering some of the federal cuts. The state program is not expected to generate more than $75 million this year, half the federal loss, so the state program was oriented towar lower-income families. Some will see the same savings they got from the federal program, while others may not be eligible for a state subsidy.

The expiration of the federal Enhanced Premium Tax Credit is expected to lead higher premiums for some 20 million Americans who directly benefited from the assistance through the Affordable Care Act. Meanwhile, the end of the tax credit has already led to increases in the private insurance market, with Maryland regulators approving an average 13.4% premium rate increase this year.

State OKs 13.4% average premium hike for state’s health care marketplace plans

That’s why lawmakers like Health and Government Operations Vice Chair Bonnie Cullison (D-Montgomery) urge Marylanders to use the Easy Enrollment option on their state tax forms to see if they qualify for more affordable health care coverage.

“The Easy Enrollment program was designed to use government processes to the absolute benefit of Marylanders,” Cullison said. “When given information from the Comptroller’s office … the exchange can quickly determine the eligibility for free or reduced health care options — or help folks compare plans that will best meet their needs.”

Vincent DeMarco with Maryland Health Care All coalition announced a $100,000 informational campaign to help uninsured Marylanders learn about the Easy Enrollment option, as those who qualify for Medicaid can still get enrolled in health care coverage.

“If you’re uninsured and you missed Open Enrollment, and you’re eligible for Medicaid – check the box at tax time and you could get enrolled,” DeMarco said. “It is especially important now.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said any effort to make access to insurance easier can help combat changes coming to health care through the Republican-controlled Congress and the Trump administration.

“Because they rolled those (expanded tax credits) back, allowed them to die at midnight on Dec. 31,” Van Hollen said, “as a result, 20 million Americans will no longer get the benefit of that tax credit. They’ll see their premiums go through the roof.”
